title: Moving to Canada, starting to teach and joining Elvin
summary: He began teaching in Toronto at Yamaha's request, moved to Canada in 1974, then Elvin called him in 1975.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Did your, your entrance into jazz education and academia, was that partly to change a lifestyle of being on the road?

I never thought I’d be — my father was a music teacher. I helped my music teacher in the school teach younger kids clarinet, never thought about teaching. Went to Potsdam State © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

Teacher’s College and never thought about teaching. Went to Berklee, it never crossed my mind. I moved to Canada in ’74 and I was with Yamaha at the time. I had signed with Yamaha in the States, the last couple of months with Buddy Rich and so when I came to Canada I was with Yamaha. And they called me and they said we’ve got this young student who is, they called him the “rising star” the Yamaha Rising Star Award. And we wondered if you’d give him a couple of lessons. I said gee, I never taught anybody. I don’t know about teaching. They said well give him a try. So I had him come by my house on Saturday mornings, and we’d go there for four hours, and I’d basically just retraced my steps of how I learned, what I did. Because I had lots of notes. I mean I had been, since being at Berklee I had all kinds of notes. I learned how to take notes. I learned how to write all my practice routines down. So I just — I listened to him play and I could see what he needed, if it was musculature, embouchure, whatever, I could see that. And then the theory about improvisation was something I had just picked up on my own through a Berklee correspondence course when I was in Potsdam I was studying the Berklee correspondence course. And all the stuff I had learned at Berklee and then with Herb Pomeroy and Ray Santisi, Charlie Mariano, basically I just retraced my steps and showed him what to do. And then there was a college here in Toronto called Humber. Humber College is the Berklee of Canada. They had the first program. Matter of fact some of the guys from Berklee came up to help them establish this school. And there was an arranger named Ron Collier, one of Canada’s most famous arrangers, one of the only guys that ever arranged for Duke Ellington and write for Duke Ellington in Canada. He started this program at Humber and they had been running about three or four years and they heard that I had taught this kid, who went eventually to this school. And they called me and asked me, they said, “Would you like to teach three more students?” I said, okay, private lessons and I wasn’t getting a lot of work. See when I first moved to Canada I couldn’t work for six months because of the union rules. You know they had a rule you couldn’t work a steady job. I was sneaking across the borders, before computers and they could check up on you, I would go back to Rochester to work Italian weddings. I’d work up north so they couldn’t trace me. You had to kind of do everything under the table. Because you weren’t allowed to work a steady gig. I had a baby on the way and so I couldn’t do it. So I took this job, and then Elvin called me in ’75, like a year later I got the call and he had been trying to get me because he because he wanted me to join, he sat in once in Buddy’s band in Ronnie Scott’s a year before. He came in and sat in and took my number to see if I was interested. But then I moved to Canada and he lost all my contact information. So he called me. And that was around 1975. So taking this part time job teaching and then Elvin called me. So I took the job with Jones and I did the part time lessons as I could throughout the semester, which was something they allowed me to do. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

I said, you know I’m going to be, I’ve got to travel to make a living here because I’m not doing anything in town. And so that’s what happened. I got the job with Elvin and then I started to get more and more students each year but it was always part time until the 80s when they offered me a — in ’87 they offered me a full time position. So I was off and on with Elvin for almost twenty years plus. I would go out with him — ’75, ’76, ’77, ’78, ’79 — I was with him pretty much. Then I left for a bit, came back, left, came back, helped him out. And then his last two years I went back for his 75th birthday tour and did two years on a sabbatical that I had taken from the school, and then he passed away in the following year.
